name: Justice Bira Kishore Ray
title: Bira Kishore Ray: Before the Court Had Its First Chief Justice
description: The lawyer, committee chairman and judge who helped carry the demand for Odisha’s own High Court into institutional life.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: When Orissa became a separate province in 1936, it did not immediately acquire a High Court of its own. The region remained within the jurisdiction of the Patna High Court, whose judges had sat on circuit at Cuttack since 1916. The distinction matters: creating a province and establishing its judicial institutions were separate tasks. Bira Kishore Ray would help carry the second task forward.

His career connected the legal profession to that institutional change. Born in 1891, he studied at Ravenshaw College and obtained his law degree from Calcutta University. In 1937 he became the new province’s first Advocate General; in 1945 he joined the bench of the Patna High Court. These appointments placed him on both sides of the transition, as a lawyer representing the province and then as a judge.

The demand for a separate court had a history beyond any one individual. Madhusudan Das had voiced hope for a permanent bench when the circuit first sat at Cuttack. In 1938 the High Court Bar Association passed a resolution seeking a separate High Court. Ray later chaired the committee appointed to examine the proposal, alongside representatives of the legislature, the bar and the administration. Its report was published at the end of 1943.

The court’s later annual report describes the committee’s case in practical terms: a separate High Court should make the administration of justice quicker and more convenient. This was an argument about the workings of a province, as well as its identity. It also reminds us that an institution begins with proposals, scrutiny and decisions before it acquires an opening date.

On 26 July 1948, Ray became the first Chief Justice of the Orissa High Court. His tenure lasted until 30 October 1951. The title gives him a distinct place in Odisha’s history, but the committee work shows that his contribution began before he occupied that office.

Remembering Ray through this sequence makes the achievement more concrete. A long-standing demand became a proposal, the proposal became a court, and its first judges then had to make the institution function. His place in that story spans the preparation and the opening years: helping make the case for a court, then taking responsibility for leading it.
